source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 2.2.6, from “Let X₁,…,X_N be independent random variables” through the displayed inequality
source_evidence.observation: The exact bounded-variable Hoeffding statement assumes X_i ∈ [m_i,M_i] for every i and, for every t > 0, gives P{∑_{i=1}^N (X_i − E X_i) ≥ t} ≤ exp(−2t²/∑_{i=1}^N (M_i−m_i)²). The displayed bound is one-sided and has no multiplicative prefactor.

Visual inspection shows absolute-value bars around the complete weighted sum: P{|∑_{i=1}^N a_iX_i| ≥ t} ≤ 2 exp(−ct²/(K²‖a‖₂²)), where K=max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}. Thus this theorem is two-sided and its right-hand side has a leading factor 2.
The weighted theorem applies to independent, mean-zero, sub-gaussian random variables X₁,…,X_N, an arbitrary vector a=(a₁,…,a_N)∈R^N, and every t≥0; c is an unspecified positive absolute constant.

The exercise asks to deduce bounded-variable Hoeffding, explicitly identified as Theorem 2.2.6, from Theorem 2.6.3, and permits “some absolute constant instead of 2 in the exponent.” It does not explicitly authorize changing the no-prefactor form of Theorem 2.2.6.

source_evidence.anchor: Definition 2.5.6 and Example 2.5.8(c), bounded random variables
source_evidence.observation: The sub-gaussian norm is defined by ‖X‖_{ψ₂}=inf{u>0:E exp(X²/u²)≤2}, and every bounded random variable satisfies ‖X‖_{ψ₂}≤C‖X‖_∞, with the displayed choice C=1/√(ln 2).

Real-valued random variables X₁,…,X_N — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6 and its real interval hypotheses.
Real interval endpoints m_i and M_i for each i=1,…,N — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, the hypotheses X_i∈[m_i,M_i].

For the exercise's permitted relaxed exponent, a positive absolute constant c₀ independent of N, t, the distributions, and the interval endpoints — PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Exercise 2.6.4’s phrase “some absolute constant instead of 2 in the exponent,” read together with Theorem 2.6.3’s absolute c.
hypotheses: X₁,…,X_N are independent random variables — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.
For every i, X_i lies in the bounded interval [m_i,M_i] — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6; the source does not explicitly say whether this notation means surely or almost surely.
No identical-distribution hypothesis and no zero-mean hypothesis are imposed on the original X_i; the conclusion centers each variable by E X_i — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.
conclusions: The exact referenced result is P{∑_{i=1}^N (X_i−E X_i)≥t}≤exp(−2t²/∑_{i=1}^N(M_i−m_i)²) for every t>0 — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.

Exercise 2.6.4 permits replacing the numerical coefficient 2 in that exponent by some positive absolute constant c₀, while its wording still points to the same one-sided centered sum and no-prefactor form — PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Exercise 2.6.4, cross-referencing Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.

A direct normalized application of the displayed Theorem 2.6.3 instead yields the two-sided estimate P{|∑_{i=1}^N(X_i−E X_i)|≥t}≤2exp(−c₁t²/∑_{i=1}^N(M_i−m_i)²) for a positive absolute c₁, and hence the same bound with leading 2 for the desired one-sided event — analyst inference from PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Theorem 2.6.3, and PDF page 16 / printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c).
definitions_and_conventions: The centered sum is S=∑_{i=1}^N(X_i−E X_i) — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.

Let b_i=M_i−m_i. For b_i>0, the normalized centered variable Y_i=(X_i−E X_i)/b_i is mean zero and satisfies |Y_i|≤1 because both X_i and E X_i lie between m_i and M_i; this normalization is an analyst inference from the interval hypothesis in Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.
Boundedness makes each normalized Y_i sub-gaussian with uniformly bounded ψ₂ norm, by ‖Y_i‖_{ψ₂}≤C‖Y_i‖_∞ — PDF page 16 / printed page 27, Definition 2.5.6 and Example 2.5.8(c).
Taking weights a_i=b_i gives ∑a_iY_i=∑(X_i−E X_i) and ‖a‖₂²=∑(M_i−m_i)² — analyst inference using the weighted form of Theorem 2.6.3 on PDF page 18 / printed page 29.

In Theorem 2.6.3, K=max_i‖Y_i‖_{ψ₂}, and all fixed numerical constants from the bounded-to-sub-gaussian estimate and Theorem 2.6.3 may be absorbed into a new positive absolute exponent constant — PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Theorem 2.6.3, and PDF page 16 / printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c).
The exact target tail event uses ≥, not >, and t is strictly positive — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.
implicit_context: All probabilities and expectations are taken with respect to the probability space carrying the X_i — structural context of Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.
The boundedness hypothesis ensures that each E X_i exists and is finite — analyst inference from X_i∈[m_i,M_i] in Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.
Measurable transformations of the independent X_i, such as their centered and scaled versions, remain independent — analyst inference needed to apply Theorem 2.6.3 on PDF page 18 / printed page 29.
The one-sided event {S≥t} is contained in the two-sided event {|S|≥t} — analyst inference connecting Theorem 2.6.3 on PDF page 18 / printed page 29 to Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.

The source uses standard interval notation and tacitly expects meaningful bounded intervals, but it states no explicit strict-positivity hypothesis on every width M_i−m_i — PDF page 6 / printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6.

details: Theorem 2.2.6 is an upper-tail inequality for the centered unweighted sum — PDF page 6 / printed page 17.
Its right-hand side is a single exponential exp(−2t²/∑(M_i−m_i)²), with no leading factor 2 — PDF page 6 / printed page 17.
Theorem 2.6.3 controls the absolute value of the complete weighted sum, not merely the upper tail; this is visible in the displayed absolute-value bars — PDF page 18 / printed page 29.

semantic_facets.topic: Normalization needed for the sum-of-squared-widths denominator
details: For positive widths b_i=M_i−m_i, applying Theorem 2.6.3 to Y_i=(X_i−E X_i)/b_i with weights a_i=b_i produces ‖a‖₂²=∑b_i² and a uniform bound on max_i‖Y_i‖_{ψ₂} — analyst inference from Theorem 2.6.3 on PDF page 18 / printed page 29 and Example 2.5.8(c) on PDF page 16 / printed page 27.

Applying the theorem directly to unnormalized centered variables with all weights equal to one would generally involve N times a maximum-width scale, not the desired sum of squared widths — analyst inference from the denominator K²‖a‖₂² in Theorem 2.6.3 on PDF page 18 / printed page 29.

Passing from the two-sided event in Theorem 2.6.3 to the desired one-sided event by event inclusion preserves the theorem's leading factor 2 — analyst inference from the displayed inequalities on PDF page 18 / printed page 29 and PDF page 6 / printed page 17.

Changing or absorbing absolute constants in the exponent does not by itself remove that leading factor uniformly for all t>0 — analyst inference from the functional forms displayed in Theorem 2.6.3 and Theorem 2.2.6.

If M_i=m_i, then the interval hypothesis forces X_i to be constant at that value under the usual probabilistic reading, so X_i−E X_i=0 and that index can be omitted from the normalized deduction — analyst inference from Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.

If some widths are positive and others are zero, normalize only the positive-width indices and discard the zero centered terms; the denominator remains the sum of all squared widths because the omitted contributions are zero — analyst inference from Theorem 2.2.6 and Theorem 2.6.3.

If every width is zero, the centered sum is identically zero and its tail probability is zero for t>0, but the displayed exponential formula contains division by a zero denominator unless an extended-real or limiting convention is supplied — analyst inference from the formula in Theorem 2.2.6 on PDF page 6 / printed page 17.

The relaxation allowed by Exercise 2.6.4 concerns an absolute exponent constant, so that constant may not depend on N, t, the particular random variables, or their interval endpoints — PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Exercise 2.6.4 and Theorem 2.6.3.

The source does not prescribe the numerical value obtained after combining the bounded-variable ψ₂ estimate with Theorem 2.6.3 — PDF page 16 / printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c), and PDF page 18 / printed page 29, Theorem 2.6.3.

ambiguities.issue: The requested deduction and the referenced target disagree on the visible multiplicative prefactor.
ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 2.2.6 has RHS exp(−2t²/∑(M_i−m_i)²) with no prefactor, while Theorem 2.6.3 has RHS 2exp(−ct²/(K²‖a‖₂²)); Exercise 2.6.4 mentions permission only to replace 2 in the exponent — PDF page 6 / printed page 17 and PDF page 18 / printed page 29.
ambiguities.impact: It is genuinely unclear whether the exercise demands the literal no-prefactor form with a changed exponent constant or accepts the immediate consequence with leading 2. The direct two-sided deduction alone establishes the latter, not the former uniformly for every t>0.

contract_plain_english: For independent real random variables X_i bounded between m_i and M_i, the exact theorem referenced by Exercise 2.6.4 says that, for every t>0, the probability that the centered sum ∑(X_i−E X_i) is at least t is at most exp(−2t²/∑(M_i−m_i)²), with no leading prefactor; the exercise permits replacing the exponent’s 2 by another positive absolute constant — PDF page 6 / printed page 17 and PDF page 18 / printed page 29. To use Theorem 2.6.3, normalize each nonconstant centered variable by its interval width and use those widths as weights; boundedness supplies a uniform sub-gaussian norm — PDF page 16 / printed page 27 and PDF page 18 / printed page 29. Visual inspection confirms that Theorem 2.6.3 controls |∑a_iX_i| and therefore directly yields a two-sided bound with leading 2; restricting that event to the upper tail retains the 2, creating a genuine source-level tension with the exact no-prefactor theorem. Singleton intervals contribute zero centered terms and can be omitted, while the case in which all intervals are singletons is probabilistically trivial but leaves the source’s displayed zero denominator without an explicit convention.
